morning_concept: 🧠 Do you know how database indexes actually work?
morning_concept_explanation:
🎯 The idea

You’ve probably heard: “Add an index and the query becomes faster.” But an index isn't just some magic accelerator. It is a separate data structure that the database maintains specifically to make certain access patterns faster.

Imagine a table with 100 million users:

users
────────────────────────
id | name | email
1  | ...  | ...
2  | ...  | ...
...
100,000,000

And you run:

SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE email = 'alice@example.com';

Without an index, the database may need to inspect a huge number of rows. That's a table scan. With an index, the database can navigate a separate search structure to find the relevant row without scanning the whole table.

🔧 How it works

For a typical PostgreSQL B-tree index, think of an ordered tree:

                 [M]
               /     \
           [D–L]     [N–Z]
           /   \      /   \
         ...   ...   ...   ...

The tree stays ordered, so the database can eliminate large parts of the search space at each step. Conceptually:

100M rows
   ↓
find the right branch
   ↓
find the right branch
   ↓
find the value
   ↓
get the row

The important idea is not memorizing “B-tree”. It's understanding that the database maintains another structure optimized for the query pattern.

🧪 A real example

Suppose we have:

orders(id, user_id, created_at, status)

And our application constantly runs:

SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 123
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

A useful index might be:

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_created
ON orders(user_id, created_at DESC);

Now the index reflects the way we're accessing the data:

user_id
   ↓
find user 123
   ↓
already ordered by created_at
   ↓
take first 20

That can avoid a large sort after retrieving the matching rows. This is why index design is really query-pattern design.

⚖️ Trade-offs

Indexes aren't free. Every index is another piece of data the database has to maintain.

More indexes
   ↓
✅ Faster some reads
   ↓
❌ More storage
❌ More work on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE

So the question isn't “Can I add an index?” It's “Which queries matter enough to justify maintaining this index?”

🧩 The subtle part: composite indexes

Suppose we create:

CREATE INDEX idx
ON users(country, age);

This is not equivalent to having two independent indexes. The order matters. A query filtering by country can use the leading part of the index, and a query filtering by country and age can use both columns effectively. A query filtering only by age does not get the same benefit because country is the first part of the index.

So when choosing (country, age) versus (age, country), start with: “What queries are we actually trying to make fast?”

💥 What can go wrong?

An index can exist and still not be used. The database has a query planner that estimates the cost of different strategies. Sometimes using the index is actually more expensive than scanning the table, especially when the query returns a large percentage of the rows.

So: “We have an index” does not mean “the database will use the index.”

🏗 Where you see it

Indexes appear everywhere: users by email, orders by user_id and time, payments by transaction_id, messages by conversation and timestamp, products by category and price. At large scale, index design becomes part of database architecture rather than just a SQL detail.

🎤 Interview connection

Database questions often start simple—“Why is this query slow?”—and then become “What if the table is 1 billion rows?”, “What if writes are much heavier?”, or “Why isn't the index being used?” The useful skill is connecting workload → access pattern → data structure → performance → read/write trade-off.

🔎 Sources
PostgreSQL documentation — indexes, B-tree indexes, multicolumn indexes, and index ordering: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes.html · https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/btree.html · https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-multicolumn.html · https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/indexes-ordering.html
evening_feedback:
🌙 Candidate Feedback

🎯 Bottom line

The useful interview trend is that strong backend interviews increasingly test whether you understand why a system behaves a certain way, rather than whether you can recite terminology.

📊 What to watch for

Database questions can start with “Why is this query slow?” and then introduce larger data, heavier writes, additional ordering, multiple filters, or a query that still doesn't use the index. The important habit is following the chain from workload → data structure → trade-off.

📚 What to do with this

When you encounter a slow database query at work, don't immediately ask “Which index should I add?” Ask: “What access pattern are we trying to optimize?” That's the habit worth keeping.

⚠️ Evidence caveat

Candidate-report datasets are signals about what people encountered, not guarantees of what any particular company will ask.
